chapter_theme: Nondi Siddhar's limping song is a first-person report of attainment: after bowing to Sivasakti and to a roll call of twenty-two siddhas he says, verse after verse, 'I knew', 'I saw', 'I reached'. The path runs from leaving chariyai and kiriyai through yoga to a silence beyond speech; the places are the body's centres (the nose-tip, the root, manipuraka, vishuddhi, the nine gates), a flight to Sathuragiri, and the gift of the goddess Manonmani, and the song closes by setting the salted pot of the body against the state the guru's word opened.
structure_note: Invocation and the lineage of siddhas (2293 to 2296); the way beyond chariyai and kiriyai and the first vision (2297 and 2298); the long run of attainments under the heading 'I saw beginning, middle and end: the state of silence' (2299 to 2315), which moves from Om and the ego to Sathuragiri, the centres, Manonmani and the body's falseness; and the opening of 'I destroyed ego: the true state' (2316 and 2317), which continues in chapter 119. Units 2299 and 2316 have three lines, the fourth being the heading the editor set as section title.

links.note: Both set Kalangi and Bogar in one line of teachers descending from Tirumular: Tirumular names Bhoga Devar among those who came from Kalangar, and Nondi's roll call runs Tirumular, Kalangi, Bogar.

Sivavakkiyar gives chariyai and kiriyai their own fruits, salokam and samipam, within a graded scheme where all four paths reach something; Nondi sets the two aside altogether and touches yoga as the means beyond them, with no fruit assigned to what he left.

Both put the goal beyond the first two paths: Arunagiri's supreme light cannot be reached by those joined to chariyai and kiriyai, and Nondi leaves them to touch the foot of yoga and finds a state he cannot tell.

Both place the Lord at a point measured from the nose-tip and beyond speech: Tirumular puts his dwelling a few finger-breadths from it, which the Veda shrinks from telling; Nondi sees the teacher's dance in the light between the eyes at the nose-tip and falls into silence.

Pattinathar's Arutpulambal says the Omkara itself perished with the ego, cut at the root; Nondi says that seeing what the pranava Om truly is brought him great good and ended the ego that says 'we'. They conflict if Pattinathar means Om is no means at all in the final state; if he means only that Om as sound dissolves there, Nondi's nadanta silence in 2312 says the same.

Both make Sathuragiri the siddhas' seat and a station on the way: Subramaniar Njanam tells the disciple to go to its summit and practise there; Nondi says he went there by the sky path and rejoiced among the siddhas of tapas.

Both credit the goddess Manonmani with giving the means: in Tirumular she wakes the sleeping yogi and gives the upaya; in Nondi it is by her grace that he knew the unknowable fullness and merged in it.

Pattinathar: the place where sound subsides is the light within Om, and that is the Brahman that stays without speaking; Nondi: he stayed in the state called the silence at the end of nada and saw the higher house. Both put the final silence where sound ends rather than in mere quiet.

Nondi's wicked 'chandalas' are company he forgot in order to find the fit vessel and join the worthy; the word marks conduct, not birth. The Kural redefines birth by conduct in the same way: having conduct is noble birth, failing in it low birth. The agreement holds if சண்டாளர் is read morally, as the stanza's contrast with பாத்திரம் suggests.

The salted pot (உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம்) for the body that dissolves: in the Meynjanap Pulambal it must break and take a womb again unless the Lord takes the speaker; in Nondi those who do not know the truth call it good and wander in bondage.

The body as a false hut or cage (பொய்க்கூடு): Arunagiri's speaker lives in the illusion that life in it is unshaken greatness; Nondi, certain it has no substance, fears and goes to a mountain cave to learn the way of Sivajnana.

Both start from the body of nine gates and make stilling or shutting them the condition of what follows: Tirumular's nine channels stilled in the one place, Nondi's gates closed before he goes through the great high path.

Sivavakkiyar seals the gates, five and four, with the final mudra and goes up the root channel past the lotus temple; Nondi realises the nine gates, closes them and goes through the great high path. The same body and the same closing before ascent.

2293.reading: Bowing daily to the feet of Ambika, the first Parapara who is Sivasakti, and taking refuge in the flower-feet of the elephant of the triangle in the faultless flame-light.
2293.nuance: திரிகோணக் குஞ்சரம், the elephant of the triangle, is Ganapati as tradition places him at the triangle of the root centre, so that the invocation is already a body-map: the Mother first, then the lord of the root. The phrase could also be read as the elephant-faced one worshipped in a triangular yantra.

2294.reading: The roll of siddhas begins: Tirumular, Kalangi, Bogar, the guru-sage of southern Pothigai, Dhanvantari, Karuvurar, Idaikkadar, Atri, Kalaikkodar, Macchamuni and Pulathiyar.
2294.nuance: குருமுனி of Pothigai is Agastya. Macchamuni (Matsyendra) appears in the list although the corpus attributes this very song to Nondi Siddhar identified with Machendranathar; either the identification is late or the poet names a predecessor of the same name. The list reads as a lineage rather than a pantheon.

2295.reading: The roll continues with Sundaranandar, Kapilar, Konganar, Sutamuni, Kosikar, Vedamuni, Nandisar and Sattaimuni, and the poet says he worshipped them and bowed at their feet.
2295.nuance: The two stanzas give twenty names, more than the usual eighteen siddhas; Nandisar stands among the human siddhas, and in 2307 he is called the poet's grandfather, the guru's guru.

2296.reading: Knowing the door of the five senses, discerning the wonder of the true way of the Brahma mantra, and parting from agitation, the poet says he resolutely bowed at the feet of the siddhas and the others.
2296.nuance: அஞ்சுபுலக் கதவு, the door of the five senses, may mean knowing how to shut them, as the nine gates are shut in 2317. பிரம மந்திரம் is unexplained; it may be the pranava of 2303 or the five letters.

2297.reading: Leaving chariyai and kiriyai and touching, beyond them, the foot of the great yoga that is the means, the transcendent appeared there, and the poet asks whether it is in his power to tell what it was to simply remain.
2297.nuance: சும்மா இருந்தது, 'simply remaining', is the Siddhars' and later Tamil mystics' phrase for the state past effort; the stanza treats it as what the verses that follow cannot really say, which sits oddly with their confident 'I saw'. உரிய அதீதம் may be 'the fitting transcendent' or 'the transcendent that is one's own'.

2298.reading: Taking hold of the Parapara space with the mind made one and fixed, seeing the arising of supreme consciousness, the poet drank fittingly the undeparting nectar of bliss, the ancient thing that rests on nothing.
2298.nuance: The syntax is loose: நிராதரமான பண்டு, 'the ancient one without support', may qualify the bliss or stand alone as the object seen. உற்பனம் (arising, manifestation) returns in 2325, where all such arisings are called imagination; the two stanzas should be read together.

2299.reading: The poet says he came to know, knew jnana, saw in full the form of the endless Parabrahman, and broke off attachment to this world.
2299.nuance: The unit has three lines; the missing first line is the heading 'I saw beginning, middle and end: the state of silence' that the editor has set as the section title. The refrain-like 'I knew, I saw' begins here and runs to 2325.

2300.reading: When the pure supreme space itself appeared as light, the poet gained the joy of true knowledge; on beholding Being, Consciousness and Bliss, that all is pervaded by Brahman is hard to put into words.
2300.nuance: சகலமும் பிரமமயம் is the Advaitic formula, rare in the earlier Siddhars and common in the later Vedantic ones. புகலரிதே, 'hard to tell', repeats the disclaimer of 2297.

2301.reading: In the supreme space that is light between the eyes, shining at the middle of the nose-tip, the poet beheld the teacher's holy dance, and the state of silence was touched.
2301.nuance: The nose-tip gaze is the classical yogic fixation; tradition takes the light seen there as the opening of the inner eye. தேசிகன், the teacher, is both Siva and the guru. பரிசமுத்தே is unclear: 'nectar of the touch' (பரிச அமுது) or 'touching, it was reached' (பரிசம் உற்றே); the reading leaves it as touched.

2302.reading: Becoming clear that thought is dream, forgetting even that thought, forgetting the rising kalai, forgetting the self that says 'mine', and renouncing the part that does not churn in the pure ocean.
2302.nuance: The stanza is a chain of forgettings in which even the knowledge that thought is dream is let go. கலை may be the arts or the breath's phases. The last line, உழலாத பாகம் துறந்தே, is obscure: perhaps leaving behind whatever does not dissolve in the pure sea, perhaps a corrupt line.

2303.reading: Having seen in truth what the pranava Om is, the poet gained great good; leaving the ego that says 'we', he found what he sought and knew his aim.
2303.nuance: நாமெனும் அகங்காரம், the ego that says 'we' rather than 'I', is a small variation on the usual தான் or நான். Knowing Om is here a gain and a means; compare the Arutpulambal, where Om itself perishes with the ego.

2304.reading: Leaving desire, given the strength to cut off the five senses that hide and run spreading out, crossing the bond and walking exactly as the guru's word said, without a step astray.
2304.nuance: The strength is given (அளித்து), not won: the one note of grace in a sequence of 'I did'. The stanza has no finite verb and runs on into 2305.

2305.reading: Taking the pill of flight and by it going deep along the sky path, the poet says he went to Sathuragiri, where the great siddhas of austerity live, and rejoiced.
2305.nuance: கவனக் குளிகை is most likely கமனக் குளிகை, the pill of going, the medicine the siddha traditions claim gives travel through the air; ககனமார்க்கம் is then the literal sky. The coded reading, as tradition takes it, makes ககனம் the inner sky and the pill the retained breath or bindu, so that the journey is in the body. Sathuragiri near Srivilliputhur is the siddhas' mountain in these songs. The stanza reports a claim, not a recipe.

2306.reading: With the lordly nine siddhas of supreme knowledge who sit on the rock of austerity, the poet knew the form of Siva, and having seen the lamp-light in his mind he broke off longing.
2306.nuance: தவசுப் பாறை is a named rock at Sathuragiri in local tradition, so the stanza can be read as a place as much as a figure. நவ சித்தர், the nine siddhas, is a smaller count than the twenty of 2294 and 2295.

2307.reading: The poet knew the root support and rejoiced to see there the lamp-light of the three flames; he learned the manifold arts, and by the grace of his grandfather Nandisar he was glad.
2307.nuance: முச்சுடர், the three flames, is the Siddhars' sun, moon and fire, read as the two breaths and the fire at the root. நாலா கலை is 'the various arts' or, forcing the number, four kalai. என் பாட்டன் நந்தீசர்: Nandi as grandfather makes Tirumular, whom 2323 calls 'our guru', the father in a lineage of three, which 2294 began.

2308.reading: Knowing the experience of yoga, the poet saw that the manipuraka is for the best a great attainment, and that remaining in the vishuddhi state so as not to die, one's own state there becomes the good state.
2308.nuance: The stanza assigns fruits to two of the six centres, the navel and the throat; tradition gives each centre its virtue, and here the throat centre carries deathlessness (சாகாது இருந்திட). The grammar of the last line is a string of nominals and the reading supplies the verbs.

2309.reading: The poet stood at what he saw, rejoiced that Sivasakti was there as imagination and went beyond; seeing the path once granted to mother Uma, he drank the intoxication of the rasa drink.
2309.nuance: ரசபானம் can be the alchemist's mercury preparation, which the siddhas claim to drink, or the inner nectar that tradition says drips from the moon in the head; the stanza's போதை (intoxication) suits either. கற்பனை அது என்று, 'that it was imagination', is hard: either Sivasakti's form is seen as a construct to be passed, or the word is corrupt.

2310.reading: Having seen the wonder of the fullness that none can know, the poet's speech subsided; by the grace of the goddess Manonmani, rich in excellence, he knew it and merged in it.
2310.nuance: பேச்சு அடங்கினேன், 'my speech subsided', is silence as an effect of seeing rather than a discipline. Manonmani, the goddess of Tirumular's Bhairavi mantra, gives the knowing here as she gives the means there.

2311.reading: Day by day the poet saw and knew the place beyond desire; he took well the name 'she is Vami', which sages and gods praise, and rose in the Supreme.
2311.nuance: வாமி is the goddess of the left, Vamadevi or Vamesvari; 'taking the name' may mean receiving her mantra, or taking her as one's deity. காமியம் கடந்த இடம், the place past desire, is the state itself, not a location.

2312.reading: Seeing the state called the silence at the end of nada, the poet stayed there, losing sleep and food; he knew the way of Vedanta and, crossing the house of ignorance, saw the higher house.
2312.nuance: நாதாந்தம் and வேதாந்தம் are two of the six ends; the stanza passes through both. உறக்கம் ஊனும் அற்றேன் may be the yogi's wakeful fast or a sign of absorption; 2324 returns to the unsleeping eye. வீடு is used twice, for the house of ignorance left and the higher house seen.

2313.reading: The poet read many sastras, forgot the company of wicked chandalas, learned to know the fit vessel, and joining those with devotion he saw release.
2313.nuance: பொல்லாச் சண்டாளர் is used for the wicked, not for a caste, and is set against பாத்திரம், the worthy vessel: a caste word turned into a word for character, which is how the Siddhars often use it. The verse values reading, unusual in a tradition that mocks book-learning.

2314.reading: This salted pot of a body came the way it came; people who do not know the truth call it good, and like those who make copper their craft they wander the land in desire and churn in bondage.
2314.nuance: உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம், the salted pot that dissolves, is Sivavakkiyar's image for the body. வந்தவழி வந்தவழி, doubled, may mean 'it goes as it came' or be a scribal repetition. செப்புக் குயமானார் is obscure: 'copper-potters', perhaps alchemists chasing gold from copper, or a corrupt phrase.

2315.reading: Certain that this body, an unstable false cage, has no substance, the poet in fear went to a mountain cave, learned the way of Sivajnana and became straight in it.
2315.nuance: அச்சமதோடு: fear is the motive for retreat, an honest detail. The body contempt here sits against 2324, where the fleshly body is kept from perishing in nishtai; the song holds both without reconciling them.

2316.reading: The poet says he abased himself as 'the knowing lame one', Nondi; he knew the fitting state and the clarity of the form of Parabrahman that the guru told.
2316.nuance: The unit has three lines; the heading 'I destroyed ego: the true state' is its missing first line. சிறந்து இழித்தேன் is a paradox, 'I excelled in lowering myself', and the name நொண்டி (lame) is taken as that self-abasement; it may also name the limping சிந்து metre of the song.

2317.reading: The poet realised himself by himself, realised the eight places and the nine gates, then shut those doors, and going through the great high path he reached the holy.
2317.nuance: ஒன்பது வாசல் are the body's nine openings; எட்டுத் தலங்கள், the eight places, is unexplained, perhaps the limbs of eightfold yoga or eight centres in the body. திரு அடைந்தேன் leaves open whether the holy reached is Siva, release or the Lady of the next verse.

source_issues: Units 2299 and 2316 have three lines each; their fourth line is the section heading the editor has lifted out as a title (அடிநடு முடிவு கண்டேன் மோனநிலை, ஆங்காரமும் ஒழித்தேன் உண்மைநிலை).
2314: வந்தவழி வந்தவழி is doubled, perhaps a scribal repetition; செப்புக் குயமானார் is obscure.
2305: கவனக் குளிகை is probably கமனக் குளிகை (the pill of flight).
2294: Macchamuni is named among the siddhas worshipped although the corpus attributes the song to Nondi Siddhar identified with Machendranathar.
